# zusbml

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zusbml/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zusbml/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zusbml/gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zusbml/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Overview

[SBML](https://sbml.org), the Systems Biology Markup Language, is how
models of biochemical networks, pharmacokinetics and cell signaling are
shared: hundreds of them are curated in [BioModels](https://www.biomodels.org/).
But an SBML file describes reactions between species in compartments, and a
solver wants `dX/dt` for each state. The translation, with amounts against
concentrations, compartments that change size, conversion factors and
events, is where hand-written versions go wrong. The R packages that read
SBML either need the libSBML system library or are no longer maintained.

zusbml reads an SBML document into one R object, writes it back as SBML,
and derives from it the equations a solver needs, with nothing but R
installed.

* **Derivation is the point.** `sbml_odes()` gives the states, their
  right-hand sides, the assignments and the events as R expressions;
  `sbml_derivs()` turns them into a function for
  [deSolve](https://cran.r-project.org/package=deSolve), with SBML's event
  semantics (delays, priorities, persistence) included.
* **Checked against the SBML Test Suite.** All 1,384 cases of the
  [SBML Test Suite](https://github.com/sbmlteam/sbml-test-suite) 3.5.0
  within the supported set reproduce their reference results under each
  case's own tolerances. The other 308 Level 3 Version 2 cases use
  algebraic rules, `delay`, fast reactions or SBML packages, and are refused
  by name rather than approximated. 1,028 of the supported cases also pass
  when read from their Level 2 Version 5 file.
* **Pure R.** The only package zusbml imports is
  [zuxml](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuxml), for the XML; there is no system
  library to install.
* **Safe with documents from anywhere.** Model math is evaluated in an
  environment built from a fixed list of base R functions, and a document
  can call only its own function definitions, so it cannot reach
  `system()` or the rest of R.
* **Round trips.** Reading, writing and reading again gives an identical
  model, for every readable Test Suite case and fifty curated BioModels.

## Installation

Once zusbml is on CRAN, install it with:

``` r
install.packages("zusbml")
```

The development version is on GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zusbml")
```

## Usage

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zusbml)
```

The package comes with a small model of a drug taken by mouth: absorbed
from the gut into the central compartment, eliminated from there, and dosed
a second time at hour 12. `sbml_read()` takes a file, a URL or the XML
itself.

```{r}
m <- sbml_read(system.file("extdata", "dosing.xml", package = "zusbml"))
m
```

Each kind of element is a data frame. The drug in the gut is an amount; the
drug in the central compartment is a concentration.

```{r}
species <- sbml_species(m)
species[, c("id", "compartment", "initial_amount", "has_only_substance_units")]
```

`sbml_odes()` derives the equations. The concentration's right-hand side is
divided by the volume of its compartment, and each reaction id stands for
its rate.

```{r}
eq <- sbml_odes(m)
eq$rhs
eq$assignments
```

`sbml_derivs()` gives deSolve what it needs, including the event: the drug
in the gut goes back up at hour 12.

```{r}
f <- sbml_derivs(m)
deSolve::ode(
  attr(f, "y0"), times = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24), func = f, parms = attr(f, "parms"),
  method = "lsodar", rootfunc = attr(f, "rootfunc"), events = attr(f, "events")
)
```

`sbml_write()` writes SBML Level 3 Version 2, and reading it back gives the
same model.

```{r}
identical(sbml_read(sbml_write(m)), m)
```

`sbml_to_rxode2()` writes the equations as
[rxode2](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rxode2) model text. rxode2 text
cannot express SBML events, so the dose at hour 12 is refused unless you
ask for it to be dropped.

```{r}
cat(sbml_to_rxode2(m, events = "drop"))
```

Functions are named `sbml_*()`: `sbml_read()` and `sbml_write()` for
documents, an accessor per element kind, and `sbml_odes()`,
`sbml_derivs()` and `sbml_to_rxode2()` for equations.

## Learn more

* [Simulating SBML models](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zusbml/articles/zusbml.html)
  walks through reading, deriving and simulating a model, with events.
* [`?zusbml`](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zusbml/reference/zusbml-package.html)
  lists what is supported and what is refused.
* The [reference index](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zusbml/reference/)
  documents every function.

## Related work

zusbml follows the
[SBML Level 3 Version 2 Core specification](https://sbml.org/documents/specifications/)
and reads Level 2 Versions 4 and 5 by mapping them to it. It is checked
against the SBML Test Suite and curated models from BioModels, neither of
which it ships. [libSBML](https://sbml.org/software/libsbml/) is the
reference implementation; zusbml does not use it.
